title: The Harmonic Oscillator
intro: A single mode of light, a microwave resonator or a mechanical vibration is a quantum harmonic oscillator. This lesson derives its evenly spaced energy levels from one commutator, then builds number states, coherent states and the truncated simulations used for continuous-variable quantum reservoirs.

blocks.text: What you need first: The Schrödinger Equation (#/quantum/dynamics/schrodinger-equation), Commutators and Compatible Observables (#/quantum/foundations/commutators) (especially $[x, p] = i$), Observables and Uncertainty (#/quantum/foundations/observables-and-uncertainty) and Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors (#/quantum/foundations/eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors). Wavefunctions, Position and Momentum (#/quantum/dynamics/wavefunctions) helps for one optional step.
What you will be able to do

items: Write the quantum Hamiltonian of an oscillator and rewrite it with ladder operators.
Derive the energy levels $E_n = \hbar\omega(n + \tfrac12)$ from one commutator, without solving a differential equation.
Act with $a$, $a^\dagger$ and $a^\dagger a$ on number states and compute averages such as $\langle x^2\rangle$.
Build a coherent state, show its photon numbers are Poisson distributed, and follow its motion in time.
Simulate an oscillator on a computer by truncating it, and check whether the truncation is safe.

blocks.text: Why the oscillator matters

Most of this shelf is about qubits: two levels, $\vert0\rangle$ and $\vert1\rangle$. The harmonic oscillator is the opposite extreme: infinitely many levels, evenly spaced. It is not an exotic system. A single mode of light in a cavity, the microwave field in a superconducting resonator, a vibrating trapped ion, the electrical oscillation in an LC circuit: all of these are harmonic oscillators, and any system jiggling gently about a stable point behaves like one. Continuous-variable quantum reservoirs (Continuous-Variable Reservoirs (#/qrc/models/continuous-variable-reservoirs)) are networks of such oscillators, and their language (photons, $a$ and $a^\dagger$, coherent states, quadratures) is what this page teaches.

The oscillator is also the best example of a beautiful trick in quantum mechanics: you can find all the energy levels using only algebra, from the single fact $[x, p] = i$. We will do that step by step.
The classical oscillator first

A mass $m$ on a spring of stiffness $k$ feels a force $F = -kx$ pulling it back towards $x = 0$. Newton's law $m\ddot{x} = -kx$ is solved by $x(t) = A\cos(\omega t + \varphi)$ with angular frequency $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$: the mass swings back and forth forever, with any amplitude $A$ you like. Its energy is kinetic plus potential,

blocks.caption: The classical oscillator's energy, with momentum p = m dx/dt. Using k = mω² puts the stiffness in terms of the frequency.

blocks.text: Worked numbers. A 0.1 kg mass on a spring with $k = 10$ N/m has $\omega = \sqrt{10/0.1} = 10$ rad/s, a period of $2\pi/10 = 0.628$ s. Pulled out 5 cm and released, it has energy $\tfrac12kA^2 = \tfrac12\times10\times0.05^2 = 0.0125$ J. Keep that number; we will compare it with the quantum energy step in a moment.

Two features carry over to quantum mechanics: the energy is a sum of a $p^2$ part and an $x^2$ part, and the frequency of oscillation does not depend on the amplitude. In the classical picture any energy from 0 upwards is allowed. That is what changes.
The quantum Hamiltonian

To make the oscillator quantum, replace position and momentum by operators $x$ and $p$ that obey the canonical commutator $[x, p] = i\hbar$ (Commutators and Compatible Observables (#/quantum/foundations/commutators)). It is the one quantum ingredient; everything else on this page follows from it. As on the rest of the shelf we set $\hbar = 1$, and we also choose units of mass and length with $m = 1$ and $\omega = 1$, so

blocks.caption: The oscillator Hamiltonian in natural units (ħ = m = ω = 1). Energies come out in units of ħω.

blocks.text: In these units, $x$ is measured in multiples of $\sqrt{\hbar/m\omega}$, the size of the oscillator's zero-point jiggle, and energy in multiples of $\hbar\omega$. To get real numbers at the end, multiply energies by $\hbar\omega$. You could now write $p = -i\,d/dx$ and solve a differential equation for the energy eigenfunctions (that route is on Wavefunctions, Position and Momentum (#/quantum/dynamics/wavefunctions)). The algebraic route is shorter and gives more.
Ladder operators

The Hamiltonian $\tfrac12(x^2 + p^2)$ looks like $\tfrac12\vert x + ip\vert^2$, which for numbers would factor as $\tfrac12(x - ip)(x + ip)$. For operators that factoring is not quite right, because $x$ and $p$ do not commute, but it is close, and the small correction is where the quantum physics lives. Define

blocks.caption: The annihilation (lowering) operator a and the creation (raising) operator a†. a is not Hermitian, so it is not an observable; it is a tool.

blocks.text: Their commutator
Step 1. Expand: $[a, a^\dagger] = \tfrac12[x + ip,\, x - ip] = \tfrac12\big([x, x] - i[x, p] + i[p, x] + [p, p]\big)$, using that the commutator is linear in each slot.
Step 2. $[x, x] = [p, p] = 0$, $[x, p] = i$ and $[p, x] = -i$. So $[a, a^\dagger] = \tfrac12\big(0 - i\cdot i + i\cdot(-i) + 0\big) = \tfrac12(1 + 1)$.

blocks.caption: The single relation from which the whole oscillator follows.

blocks.text: The Hamiltonian in terms of a and a†
Step 1. Multiply: $a^\dagger a = \tfrac12(x - ip)(x + ip) = \tfrac12(x^2 + ixp - ipx + p^2)$. Keep the order of $x$ and $p$; that is the whole point.
Step 2. The middle terms are $i(xp - px) = i[x, p] = i\cdot i = -1$. So $a^\dagger a = \tfrac12(x^2 + p^2) - \tfrac12$.
Step 3. Rearranged:

blocks.tex: H = a^\dagger a + \tfrac12 = N + \tfrac12, \qquad N = a^\dagger a
blocks.caption: N is the number operator. The extra 1/2 came from x and p not commuting: it is the zero-point energy.

blocks.text: So finding the energies of $H$ is the same as finding the eigenvalues of $N$. Its name will be explained shortly: it counts.

blocks.title: Check yourself: the other order
blocks.text: Express $aa^\dagger$ in terms of $N$, and so write $H$ using $aa^\dagger$ instead.
solution: From $[a, a^\dagger] = aa^\dagger - a^\dagger a = 1$: $aa^\dagger = a^\dagger a + 1 = N + 1$.

blocks.text: The energy levels, derived
Now we find every eigenvalue of $N$ using only $[a, a^\dagger] = 1$. Follow the steps; each is short.

Step 1. Commutators of $N$ with the ladder operators. Using the product rule for commutators, $[AB, C] = A[B, C] + [A, C]B$: $[N, a] = [a^\dagger a, a] = a^\dagger[a, a] + [a^\dagger, a]a = 0 - a = -a$. Similarly $[N, a^\dagger] = a^\dagger[a, a^\dagger] + [a^\dagger, a^\dagger]a = a^\dagger$.

blocks.tex: N\vert n\rangle = n\vert n\rangle, \qquad E_n = n + \tfrac12 \quad (n = 0, 1, 2, \dots), \qquad\text{in ordinary units } E_n = \hbar\omega\left(n + \tfrac12\right)
blocks.caption: The oscillator's energy levels: an evenly spaced ladder starting at the zero-point energy ħω/2.

blocks.alt: A parabolic potential with five evenly spaced horizontal energy levels labelled |0> to |4> with energies n + 1/2; a green upward arrow labelled a-dagger and a red downward arrow labelled a connect neighbouring levels.
blocks.caption: The oscillator's evenly spaced ladder of number states. The creation operator a† steps up one level and the annihilation operator a steps down one.

blocks.text: Two things are new compared with the classical oscillator. The energy is quantised: it comes only in steps of $\hbar\omega$, and in a photonic system $n$ is literally the number of photons, each carrying $\hbar\omega$. And the lowest energy is not zero but $\tfrac12\hbar\omega$: even in its ground state the oscillator cannot sit still at $x = 0$ with $p = 0$, because that would violate the uncertainty relation.

Worked numbers. For the 10 rad/s spring above, $\hbar\omega = 1.055\times10^{-34}\times10 = 1.05\times10^{-33}$ J. Its classical energy of 0.0125 J is about $1.2\times10^{31}$ quanta, so steps of one quantum are utterly invisible, which is why springs look classical. For a superconducting microwave resonator at 5 GHz, one quantum is $hf = 6.626\times10^{-34}\times5\times10^9 = 3.3\times10^{-24}$ J, which in temperature units ($E/k_B$) is 0.24 K. Cooled in a dilution refrigerator to 20 mK, the resonator's mean thermal photon number $\bar n = 1/(e^{hf/k_BT} - 1)$ is $6\times10^{-6}$: it sits in its ground state, and single quanta matter. At 100 mK, $\bar n$ is already 0.10.

Notation clash: $\vert0\rangle$ and $\vert1\rangle$ here are the vacuum and the one-photon state, not qubit states. Context always makes it clear, and the QRC continuous-variable page uses the oscillator meaning.

blocks.title: Check yourself: energies
blocks.text: In natural units, what are the energies of $\vert0\rangle$, $\vert3\rangle$, and the gap between any two neighbouring levels? What energy (in joules) does a 5 GHz resonator lose when it drops from $\vert3\rangle$ to $\vert1\rangle$?
solution: $\vert3\rangle \to \vert1\rangle$ is two steps: $2hf = 2\times3.3\times10^{-24} = 6.6\times10^{-24}$ J, emitted as two photons' worth of energy.

blocks.text: Number states and how the ladder operators act
We know $a\vert n\rangle$ is proportional to $\vert n - 1\rangle$; now we find the constant, so we can compute with these states.

Step 1. Write $a\vert n\rangle = c\,\vert n - 1\rangle$. Its squared length is $\vert c\vert^2$ (since $\vert n - 1\rangle$ is normalised), and by Step 4 above it is also $\langle n\vert N\vert n\rangle = n$. So $\vert c\vert = \sqrt n$, and we choose the phase so that $c = \sqrt n$.

Step 2. Similarly $a^\dagger\vert n\rangle = d\,\vert n + 1\rangle$ with $\vert d\vert^2 = \langle n\vert aa^\dagger\vert n\rangle = \langle n\vert(N + 1)\vert n\rangle = n + 1$, so $d = \sqrt{n + 1}$.

blocks.tex: a\vert n\rangle = \sqrt n\,\vert n-1\rangle, \qquad a^\dagger\vert n\rangle = \sqrt{n+1}\,\vert n+1\rangle, \qquad a\vert0\rangle = 0
blocks.caption: How the ladder operators act on number (Fock) states.

blocks.text: Step 3. Every number state can be built from the vacuum by raising: $\vert1\rangle = a^\dagger\vert0\rangle$, $\vert2\rangle = a^\dagger\vert1\rangle/\sqrt2$, and in general $\vert n\rangle = (a^\dagger)^n\vert0\rangle/\sqrt{n!}$. The $\sqrt{n!}$ collects the factors $\sqrt1\sqrt2\cdots\sqrt n$ picked up on the way.

Step 4. As matrices in the basis $\vert0\rangle, \vert1\rangle, \vert2\rangle, \dots$: $a = \sum_n \sqrt n\,\vert n - 1\rangle\langle n\vert$ has the numbers $\sqrt1, \sqrt2, \sqrt3, \dots$ just above the diagonal and zeros elsewhere. Kept to three levels its rows are $(0, 1, 0)$, $(0, 0, 1.414)$, $(0, 0, 0)$. Its transpose $a^\dagger$ has them just below the diagonal, and $N = a^\dagger a$ is diagonal with entries $0, 1, 2, \dots$
Worked example: position spread of a number state
How spread out in position is the oscillator in state $\vert n\rangle$? We need $\langle x\rangle$ and $\langle x^2\rangle$.
Step 1. Invert the definitions: $x = (a + a^\dagger)/\sqrt2$ and $p = i(a^\dagger - a)/\sqrt2$.

Step 2. $\langle n\vert x\vert n\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(\sqrt n\langle n\vert n - 1\rangle + \sqrt{n + 1}\langle n\vert n + 1\rangle\big) = 0$, because different number states are orthogonal. A number state is centred on $x = 0$.

Step 3. $x^2 = \tfrac12(a + a^\dagger)^2 = \tfrac12(a^2 + a^{\dagger2} + aa^\dagger + a^\dagger a)$. The terms $a^2$ and $a^{\dagger2}$ change $n$ by two, so their averages in $\vert n\rangle$ vanish. What remains: $\langle x^2\rangle = \tfrac12(\langle aa^\dagger\rangle + \langle a^\dagger a\rangle) = \tfrac12\big((n + 1) + n\big) = n + \tfrac12$.

Step 4. So the variance of position is $n + \tfrac12$; the same steps give $\langle p^2\rangle = n + \tfrac12$. For the vacuum both are $\tfrac12$ and their product of standard deviations is $\sigma_x\sigma_p = \tfrac12$, exactly the minimum allowed by the uncertainty relation $\sigma_x\sigma_p \ge \tfrac12$ (Observables and Uncertainty (#/quantum/foundations/observables-and-uncertainty)). Higher number states are more spread out, and for $\vert1\rangle$, $\langle x^2\rangle = 1.5$. Check: the energy is $\tfrac12\langle p^2\rangle + \tfrac12\langle x^2\rangle = n + \tfrac12$, as it must be.

Optional, using Wavefunctions, Position and Momentum (#/quantum/dynamics/wavefunctions): in position space $p = -i\,d/dx$, so $a = (x + d/dx)/\sqrt2$ and the condition $a\vert0\rangle = 0$ becomes $\psi_0'(x) = -x\,\psi_0(x)$, solved by the Gaussian $\psi_0(x) = \pi^{-1/4}e^{-x^2/2}$ (the constant makes $\int\vert\psi_0\vert^2dx = 1$, since $\int e^{-x^2}dx = \sqrt\pi$). The ground state is a bell curve of width about 1 in natural units.

blocks.title: Check yourself: ladder arithmetic
blocks.text: Compute $a^\dagger\vert2\rangle$, $a\vert2\rangle$, $a^\dagger a\vert2\rangle$, and $a^2\vert3\rangle$.
solution: $a^\dagger a\vert2\rangle = a^\dagger\sqrt2\vert1\rangle = \sqrt2\sqrt2\vert2\rangle = 2\vert2\rangle$: the number operator counts.

blocks.text: Coherent states: the quantum version of a swinging mass

A number state does not oscillate at all: $\langle x\rangle = 0$ at every time, because an energy eigenstate only gains a phase (The Schrödinger Equation (#/quantum/dynamics/schrodinger-equation)). So where is the swinging mass? It is in a superposition of many number states, and the most classical such superposition is the coherent state. A laser beam, or a resonator driven by a steady microwave tone, is in (very nearly) a coherent state.

Definition: a coherent state $\vert\alpha\rangle$ is an eigenstate of the lowering operator, $a\vert\alpha\rangle = \alpha\vert\alpha\rangle$, where $\alpha$ is any complex number. (Since $a$ is not Hermitian, its eigenvalues can be complex.) Let us find it.

Step 1. Expand in number states, $\vert\alpha\rangle = \sum_n c_n\vert n\rangle$. Then $a\vert\alpha\rangle = \sum_n c_n\sqrt n\,\vert n - 1\rangle = \sum_n c_{n+1}\sqrt{n + 1}\,\vert n\rangle$ (shifting the label).

Step 2. Matching the coefficient of $\vert n\rangle$ with $\alpha c_n$: $c_{n+1}\sqrt{n + 1} = \alpha c_n$, so $c_{n+1} = \alpha c_n/\sqrt{n + 1}$. Applying this repeatedly: $c_1 = \alpha c_0$, $c_2 = \alpha^2c_0/\sqrt{2}$, ..., $c_n = \alpha^nc_0/\sqrt{n!}$.

Step 3. Normalise: $\sum_n\vert c_n\vert^2 = \vert c_0\vert^2\sum_n\vert\alpha\vert^{2n}/n! = \vert c_0\vert^2e^{\vert\alpha\vert^2} = 1$, using the series $e^y = \sum y^n/n!$. So $c_0 = e^{-\vert\alpha\vert^2/2}$.

blocks.caption: A coherent state and its photon-number distribution, a Poisson distribution with mean |α|².

blocks.text: Worked example: photon counting with alpha = 2
Step 1. $\vert\alpha\vert^2 = 4$, so $P(n) = e^{-4}4^n/n!$.

Step 2. $P(0) = e^{-4} = 0.0183$, $P(1) = 0.0733$, $P(2) = 0.1465$, $P(3) = 0.1954$, $P(4) = 0.1954$, $P(5) = 0.1563$, $P(6) = 0.1042$, $P(7) = 0.0595$. The most likely counts are 3 and 4, and there is under 2% chance of finding the oscillator empty.

Step 3. The mean photon number: $\langle n\rangle = \langle\alpha\vert a^\dagger a\vert\alpha\rangle$. Since $a\vert\alpha\rangle = \alpha\vert\alpha\rangle$ and, taking the adjoint, $\langle\alpha\vert a^\dagger = \alpha^*\langle\alpha\vert$, this is $\alpha^*\alpha = \vert\alpha\vert^2 = 4$.

Step 4. The spread: $\langle n^2\rangle = \langle a^\dagger aa^\dagger a\rangle = \langle a^\dagger(a^\dagger a + 1)a\rangle = \langle a^{\dagger2}a^2\rangle + \langle a^\dagger a\rangle = \vert\alpha\vert^4 + \vert\alpha\vert^2$. So the variance is $\vert\alpha\vert^2 = 4$, standard deviation 2, equal to the mean, the signature of a Poisson distribution.
How a coherent state moves

Step 1. Each number state evolves by a phase: $\vert n\rangle \to e^{-i(n + 1/2)t}\vert n\rangle$. So $c_n = e^{-\vert\alpha\vert^2/2}\alpha^n/\sqrt{n!}$ becomes $e^{-it/2}e^{-\vert\alpha\vert^2/2}(\alpha e^{-it})^n/\sqrt{n!}$.

Step 2. Apart from the overall phase $e^{-it/2}$, which has no effect, that is the coherent state with label $\alpha e^{-it}$. A coherent state stays coherent; its label just rotates in the complex plane at the oscillator frequency.

Step 3. Its average position is $\langle x\rangle = \langle(a + a^\dagger)\rangle/\sqrt2 = (\alpha + \alpha^*)/\sqrt2 = \sqrt2\,\mathrm{Re}\,\alpha$. With $\alpha(t) = 2e^{-it}$: $\langle x\rangle(t) = 2\sqrt2\cos t$, a swing of amplitude 2.83 at frequency $\omega$, exactly the classical motion. Meanwhile the variances stay at the vacuum value $\tfrac12$ (the sample checks this), so the state is a minimum-uncertainty blob riding along the classical orbit.

For an oscillator of light, $x$ and $p$ are called the quadratures; they are what homodyne detection measures directly, giving a continuous outcome rather than a photon count. Squeezed states trade noise between them: one variance below $\tfrac12$, the other above, with the product still at least $\tfrac14$.

blocks.title: Check yourself: vacuum probability
blocks.text: A coherent state has $\alpha = 1.5 + 0.5i$. What are its mean photon number and the probability of finding no photons?
Coherent versus thermal light

A thermal state with the same mean photon number $\bar n$ looks completely different: $P(n) = \bar n^n/(\bar n + 1)^{n+1}$, a falling geometric distribution whose most likely value is always zero, with variance $\bar n + \bar n^2$. For $\bar n = 4$: $P(0) = 0.2$, $P(1) = 0.16$, $P(2) = 0.128$, each one 0.8 times the one before. A coherent state is a definite oscillation with a well-defined phase; a thermal state is a random jumble with no phase at all. The widget compares the two.

widget.title: Photon numbers of a coherent state

blocks.text: Try this. (1) Leave $\vert\alpha\vert = 2$: the coherent (Poisson) stems peak at 3 and 4 with $P(0) = 0.018$, as in the worked example, while the thermal stems start at $P(0) = 0.2$ and fall. (2) Set $\vert\alpha\vert$ to 0.5: both distributions are almost all at $n = 0$ and look alike; with very few photons the difference is hard to see. (3) Raise $\vert\alpha\vert$ to 4: the Poisson peak moves to about 16 photons with a spread of about 4, and with the largest $n$ shown at 20 you can see it being cut off; set the largest $n$ shown to 40 and the whole distribution appears. Keeping too few levels is exactly the truncation problem of the next section.
Simulating an infinite ladder on a computer

A computer cannot store infinitely many amplitudes. Simulations keep only the levels $\vert0\rangle, \dots, \vert N - 1\rangle$ and build $a$ as an $N\times N$ matrix with $\sqrt1, \dots, \sqrt{N - 1}$ above the diagonal. This truncation is an approximation, and you must know where it fails.

Step 1. In the truncated space, compute $aa^\dagger - a^\dagger a$. On every level below the top it is 1, as it should be. On the top level $\vert N - 1\rangle$, $a^\dagger$ would need to go to $\vert N\rangle$, which is missing, so $aa^\dagger$ gives 0 there while $a^\dagger a$ gives $N - 1$: the commutator's last diagonal entry is $-(N - 1)$, badly wrong.

Step 2. So the truncation is fine as long as the state never puts appreciable weight on the top levels. For a coherent state you can estimate the lost weight from the Poisson tail: with $\vert\alpha\vert^2 = 2.5$ and $N = 10$ levels, $P(n \ge 10) = 2.8\times10^{-4}$; with $N = 15$, $6.9\times10^{-8}$. With $\vert\alpha\vert^2 = 16$, even 20 levels lose 19% of the state, and 30 levels still lose 0.11%.

Step 3. The practical rule: run your simulation, then check the population of the top level (or top few). If it is above your tolerance, increase $N$ and run again. A dynamics that pumps energy in (a drive) needs more levels as time goes on; one with loss settles down.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from math import factorial
N = 30                                          # Fock-space truncation |0> ... |N-1>
a = np.diag(np.sqrt(np.arange(1, N)), 1); ad = a.T; num = ad @ a
comm = a @ ad - ad @ a
print("[a, a^dagger] = 1 on the first N-1 levels:", np.allclose(np.diag(comm)[:-1], 1),
      "| last diagonal entry:", round(np.diag(comm)[-1], 3), "(a truncation artefact)")
print("number operator eigenvalues 0..4:", np.diag(num)[:5])
# Coherent state |alpha>: Poisson photon numbers, <a> = alpha
alpha = 1.5 + 0.5j
c = np.array([np.exp(-abs(alpha)**2 / 2) * alpha**n / float(factorial(n)) ** 0.5 for n in range(N)])
print("norm:", round(np.linalg.norm(c), 6), " <a> =", np.round(np.vdot(c, a @ c), 4),
      " <n> =", round(np.vdot(c, num @ c).real, 4), " |alpha|^2 =", abs(alpha)**2)
x = (a + ad) / np.sqrt(2); p = 1j * (ad - a) / np.sqrt(2)
var = lambda O: (np.vdot(c, O @ O @ c) - np.vdot(c, O @ c) ** 2).real
print("Var x =", round(var(x), 4), " Var p =", round(var(p), 4), " (vacuum value 1/2 each)")
# Energy levels of H = a^dagger a + 1/2 are evenly spaced
print("lowest energies:", np.round(np.linalg.eigvalsh(num + 0.5 * np.eye(N))[:4], 3))

blocks.text: Output of the run: with 30 levels, $[a, a^\dagger] = 1$ on the first 29 levels and the last diagonal entry is $-29$, the truncation artefact. The number operator has eigenvalues 0 to 4 on the first five levels. The coherent state with $\alpha = 1.5 + 0.5i$ is normalised, has $\langle a\rangle = \alpha$ and $\langle n\rangle = 2.5 = \vert\alpha\vert^2$, and quadrature variances of exactly 0.5. The lowest energies are 0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5.

The second sample follows a coherent state in time inside a truncated space and checks the claims of this page: the classical swing of $\langle x\rangle$, the constant variance, and what happens when the truncation is too small.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from math import factorial
from scipy.linalg import expm
def ladder(N):
    a = np.diag(np.sqrt(np.arange(1, N)), 1).astype(complex)
    return a, a.conj().T
def coherent(alpha, N):
    return np.array([np.exp(-abs(alpha)**2 / 2) * alpha**n / np.sqrt(float(factorial(n))) for n in range(N)], complex)
N = 40
a, ad = ladder(N); x = (a + ad) / np.sqrt(2); H = ad @ a + 0.5 * np.eye(N)
# <x^2> in number states is n + 1/2
for n in range(3):
    v = np.zeros(N); v[n] = 1
    print(f"<{n}| x^2 |{n}> = {v @ (x @ x).real @ v:.3f}")
# A coherent state with alpha = 2 swings like the classical oscillator, with constant variance 1/2
psi0 = coherent(2.0, N)
for t in (0.0, np.pi / 4, np.pi / 2, np.pi):
    psi = expm(-1j * H * t) @ psi0
    mx = np.vdot(psi, x @ psi).real; vx = np.vdot(psi, x @ x @ psi).real - mx**2
    print(f"t={t:5.3f}: <x> = {mx:+.4f} (classical 2*sqrt2*cos t = {2*np.sqrt(2)*np.cos(t):+.4f}), Var x = {vx:.4f}")
# Truncation check: weight on the top level and the error in <n> for |alpha|^2 = 16
for Nt in (20, 30, 40):
    c = coherent(4.0, Nt)
    print(f"N={Nt}: kept norm^2 = {np.sum(abs(c)**2):.5f}, top-level population = {abs(c[-1])**2:.2e}")

blocks.text: Output of the run: $\langle n\vert x^2\vert n\rangle$ is 0.500, 1.500 and 2.500 for $n = 0, 1, 2$. The coherent state with $\alpha = 2$ has $\langle x\rangle = +2.8284, +2.0000, 0.0000, -2.8284$ at $t = 0, \pi/4, \pi/2, \pi$, matching $2\sqrt2\cos t$, and $\mathrm{Var}\,x = 0.5000$ at every time. For $\vert\alpha\vert = 4$, 20 levels keep only 81.2% of the state (top-level population $7.0\times10^{-2}$, a clear warning), 30 levels keep 99.89% (top level $1.1\times10^{-3}$), and 40 levels keep all but a few parts in a million (top level $5.0\times10^{-7}$).

blocks.title: Check yourself: is 10 levels enough?
blocks.text: You simulate a coherent state with $\vert\alpha\vert^2 = 2.5$. Is a truncation at 10 levels safe, judging by the Poisson tail?
solution: $P(n\ge10)$ for a Poisson distribution of mean 2.5 is about $2.8\times10^{-4}$.
That is small but not negligible for precise work; 15 levels bring it below $10^{-7}$. The safe rule: check the population of the top level stays below your tolerance.

blocks.text: Putting it together

Problem. A 5 GHz microwave resonator is driven into the coherent state $\alpha = 3$. (a) Mean photon number and its standard deviation? (b) Energy above the ground state, in joules? (c) Probability of measuring exactly 9 photons? (d) How many Fock levels would you keep to simulate it with less than $10^{-6}$ of the state lost?
Step 1. $\langle n\rangle = \vert\alpha\vert^2 = 9$, standard deviation $\sqrt9 = 3$.
Step 2. The energy above the ground state is $\langle n\rangle hf = 9\times3.3\times10^{-24} = 3.0\times10^{-23}$ J.
Step 3. $P(9) = e^{-9}9^9/9! = 0.132$: even at the mean, only about one measurement in eight gives exactly 9.

Step 4. The Poisson tail with mean 9 falls below $10^{-6}$ at $n = 27$ (computed: $P(n \ge 27) = 9.6\times10^{-7}$, while $P(n \ge 26) = 2.9\times10^{-6}$), so keep 27 levels, $\vert0\rangle$ to $\vert26\rangle$; then check the top-level population in the simulation.
Key points

items: The oscillator Hamiltonian is $H = \tfrac12(p^2 + x^2)$ in natural units, and $[x, p] = i$ is its only quantum ingredient.
With $a = (x + ip)/\sqrt2$: $[a, a^\dagger] = 1$ and $H = a^\dagger a + \tfrac12$.
The algebra alone forces the levels $E_n = \hbar\omega(n + \tfrac12)$, $n = 0, 1, 2, \dots$: evenly spaced, with a zero-point energy $\hbar\omega/2$.
$a\vert n\rangle = \sqrt n\vert n - 1\rangle$, $a^\dagger\vert n\rangle = \sqrt{n + 1}\vert n + 1\rangle$; $a^\dagger a$ counts quanta (photons).

Number states do not move; coherent states $\vert\alpha\rangle$ (eigenstates of $a$) follow the classical orbit with vacuum-sized noise, and their photon numbers are Poisson with mean and variance $\vert\alpha\vert^2$.
Simulations truncate to $N$ levels; the commutator fails on the top level, so always check the top-level population.

blocks.text: Problems

blocks.title: Ladder arithmetic
blocks.text: Compute $(a^\dagger)^2\vert1\rangle$ and $\langle2\vert a^\dagger a^\dagger a\vert2\rangle$.
blocks.hint: Act one operator at a time from the right.

blocks.title: Vacuum probability of a coherent state
blocks.text: For $\alpha = 2$, what are the mean photon number and the probability of finding no photons?

blocks.title: Uncertainty of a number state
blocks.text: Compute $\sigma_x\sigma_p$ for $\vert2\rangle$. Is it a minimum-uncertainty state?
blocks.hint: Use $\langle x^2\rangle = n + \tfrac12$ from the worked example.
solution: $\langle x\rangle = \langle p\rangle = 0$, and $\langle x^2\rangle = \langle p^2\rangle = n + \tfrac12 = 2.5$.
So $\sigma_x = \sigma_p = \sqrt{2.5}$ and $\sigma_x\sigma_p = 2.5$, five times the minimum $\tfrac12$. Only the vacuum (and coherent states) reach the minimum.

blocks.title: Thermal photons in a resonator
blocks.text: A 5 GHz resonator ($hf/k_B = 0.24$ K) is at 50 mK. What is its mean thermal photon number, and what is the probability it holds at least one photon?
solution: For a thermal state $P(0) = 1/(\bar n + 1)$, so $P(n \ge 1) = 1 - 1/1.0083 = \bar n/(\bar n + 1) = 0.0082$.

blocks.title: A quarter period later
blocks.text: An oscillator starts in the coherent state $\alpha = 2$ (real). What are $\langle x\rangle$ and $\langle p\rangle$ at $t = \pi/2$ (a quarter period, natural units)?
solution: $\langle p\rangle = \langle i(a^\dagger - a)\rangle/\sqrt2 = i(\alpha^* - \alpha)/\sqrt2 = \sqrt2\,\mathrm{Im}\,\alpha = \sqrt2\times(-2) = -2.83$. The mass is at the centre, moving at full speed in the negative direction, as a classical one would be.
